Panel: AI Automation, Worker Transition, and Company-Level Action

Asking your help. Detail and sources

Each card shows the chart exactly as captured from the source's published page, with the live URL beneath.

1.CEO-to-worker pay ratio, 1965–2024
Macro context

What it shows: EPI's Figure A from the most recent annual CEO Pay report. Two measures of CEO-to-typical-worker compensation ratio over six decades: Realized (dark line, including stock vested) and Granted (light line, including stock granted but not yet vested). Realized hits 280.7× in 2024, vs. 20.6× in 1965, with a peak of 393.1× in 2000.

Why it might matter: Pre-dates AI but sets the inequality baseline AI is being layered onto. Useful as opening context.

Source: Economic Policy Institute, "CEO Pay in 2023" Figure A · epi.org/publication/ceo-pay-in-2023 · epi.org/publication/ceo-pay
2.Productivity-pay gap, 1948–2025
Macro context

What it shows: Net productivity vs. hourly compensation of a typical worker, indexed to 1948 = 100. Tracked together until ~1979, then diverged sharply. EPI's annotations give average annual growth: 1948–79 productivity 2.5% / compensation 2.1%; 1979–2025 productivity 1.4% / compensation 0.6%.

Why it might matter: Frames AI as an accelerator of a 45-year decoupling, not a new phenomenon.

Source: Economic Policy Institute · epi.org/productivity-pay-gap
3.Income share of the richest 1% (United States, 1913–2024)
Macro context

What it shows: Pre-tax national income share captured by the top 1% in the U.S. from 1913 to 2024. The U-shape: ~20%+ in the 1920s, down to ~10% by the late 1970s, back above 20% today. Source data: World Inequality Database.

Why it might matter: Direct view of where productivity gains have actually gone over the long run.

Source: Our World in Data (data: World Inequality Database) · ourworldindata.org/.../income-share-top-1-before-tax-wid?country=~USA
Caveat: Captured chart shows top-1% only (no bottom-50% line on this view). The OWID grapher supports adding metrics; wid.world for matched top/bottom comparisons.
4.Distribution of household wealth in the U.S. since 1989
Macro context

What it shows: Federal Reserve Distributional Financial Accounts: share of household wealth held by Top 0.1%, 99–99.9%, 90–99%, 50–90%, and Bottom 50% from 1989 to 2025. Bottom 50% is a thin sliver across the whole range.

Why it might matter: AI-driven returns flow primarily to capital. If "who benefits from automation" is the question, the existing wealth distribution is most of the answer.

Source: Federal Reserve Board, Distributional Financial Accounts · federalreserve.gov/releases/z1/dataviz/dfa/distribute/chart/
5.Living wage vs. typical wages — North Carolina
Macro context

What it shows: MIT Living Wage Calculator for NC: living-wage / poverty-wage / minimum-wage broken out for household types from "1 adult" through "2 adults + 3 children", alongside typical-expenses and typical-annual-salaries-by-occupation tables.

Why it might matter: Localizes the abstract inequality debate to NC specifically. Concretizes "even employed people are vulnerable."

Source: MIT Living Wage Calculator · livingwage.mit.edu/states/37
Caveat: MIT publishes this dataset as tables, not charts. County-level pages exist (e.g. Durham: livingwage.mit.edu/counties/37063) for tighter geographic frames.
6.AI's effect on early-career employment in AI-exposed jobs
AI-specific

What it shows: Normalized headcount by age cohort 2021–2025 for two AI-exposed jobs: software developers and customer-support agents. The 22–25 (early-career) cohort declines sharply for software developers; mid-career (31–34, 35–40) and senior (50+) cohorts hold flat or grow. Customer-support agents show a milder version of the same pattern.

Why it might matter: One of the first empirical signals that AI is not just lifting wages for the AI-skilled — it's hollowing out entry-level slots in AI-exposed occupations right now. Direct relevance to a university audience whose graduates enter at exactly this rung.

Source: Stanford AI Index 2026, Figure 4.4.29 (Brynjolfsson et al.) · hai.stanford.edu/ai-index/2026-ai-index-report/economy
7.Fastest-growing and fastest-declining jobs, 2025–2030
AI-specific

What it shows: WEF Future of Jobs Report 2025, Figure 2.2: top 15 fastest-growing roles (led by Big Data Specialists, FinTech Engineers, AI/ML Specialists, Software Developers) and top 15 fastest-declining roles (Postal Service Clerks, Bank Tellers, Cashiers, Administrative Assistants), by net growth % 2025–2030. Growing roles up to ~110% net; declining down to roughly −40%.

Why it might matter: Forces the conversation from "if" to "where" and "how fast", with named roles. Useful when audience members assume their sector is safe.

Source: World Economic Forum, Future of Jobs Report 2025 (Figure 2.2, p. 19) · weforum.org/.../future-of-jobs-report-2025/in-full/2-jobs-outlook/ · reports.weforum.org/.../WEF_Future_of_Jobs_Report_2025.pdf
8.AI usage by job type — Anthropic Economic Index
AI-specific

What it shows: For ~24 U.S. BLS occupational categories, the share of Claude conversations (orange) vs the share of U.S. workers (grey). "Computer and mathematical" is the largest gap (37.2% of Claude conversations vs 3.4% of US workers). Arts/design/media: 10.3% vs 1.4%. Office and administrative support is under-represented relative to its workforce share.

Why it might matter: One of the few empirical (not survey-based) views of where AI is actually landing in the labor market right now. Pairs especially well with #6 — Computer/Mathematical is the most AI-saturated occupation AND where junior software developer headcount is dropping.

Source: Anthropic, "Introducing the Anthropic Economic Index" · anthropic.com/news/the-anthropic-economic-index
9.Cost to replace a worker (Gallup)
Company action

What it shows: Gallup's headline finding: voluntary turnover costs U.S. businesses ~$1 trillion/year, and replacing a single employee costs between one-half and two times their annual salary.

Why it might matter: Pivots the discussion from "should companies help displaced workers" to "is it actually cheaper to" — a different argument. Gallup's 0.5×–2× salary figure is the most-cited public benchmark for replacement cost.

Source: Gallup, "This Fixable Problem Costs U.S. Businesses $1 Trillion" · gallup.com/.../fixable-problem-costs-businesses-trillion
Caveat: Gallup presents the figure as a stat callout rather than a chart — the screenshot is the source page. The Center for American Progress 2012 paper "There Are Significant Business Costs to Replacing Employees" (americanprogress.org) has a chart-based version of the same data, broken out by salary band.
10.Reskilling demand — "If the global workforce were 100 people…"
Company action

What it shows: WEF infographic — of 100 global workers by 2030: 41 would not need upskilling, 29 would be upskilled in their current role, 19 would be upskilled and re-deployed, 11 would be unlikely to receive the necessary upskilling.

Why it might matter: Quantifies why "individuals should just retrain" is structurally insufficient — and where institutions (Duke included) sit in the gap. The "59 of 100 need training" framing tracks the brief's intent.

Source: WEF Future of Jobs Report 2025 · weforum.org/.../future-of-jobs-report-2025/infographics-94b6214b36/

Other candidates worth considering

  • GDP per capita vs. median household income — shows the "GDP illusion" where macro growth doesn't reach the median household. (FRED + Census)
  • Long-term performance of high-road employers — JUST Capital's rankings track stock performance and worker outcomes for companies rated on labor practices.
  • Profit-sharing / co-determination case studies — comparative institutional setups (German Mitbestimmung, Patagonia, Costco, Publix ESOP) and their outcomes on retention and productivity.
  • Local-area outcomes after major-employer automation — Brookings and regional Federal Reserve studies on Rust Belt and Southern manufacturing transitions.
  • Apprenticeship and community college throughput in NC — NC Community Colleges + ApprenticeshipNC publish enrollment and completion data; useful for the regional capacity question.
  • PwC AI Jobs Barometer wage-premium figure — 56% wage premium for AI-skilled workers; complement to #6 if you want both the wage-premium and the early-career-displacement angles.

Where these graphs commonly lead — for context

Not recommendations — just a sketch of the kinds of company-level moves the literature pairs with these graphs, in case it helps decide which graphs frame which conversation.

LeverWhat it isGraphs commonly cited
Internal mobility / reskilling When automating a role, fund the worker's transition into an adjacent role rather than backfilling externally. #9 (replacement cost), #10 (reskilling gap)
Productivity-gain sharing A defined share of automation-driven productivity gains flows back to affected workers (bonus, wage floor, profit-share). #2 (productivity-pay gap), #6 (early-career displacement)
Job-ladder preservation When automating mid-level work, keep entry-level intact and promote into the gap rather than hollow out the pipeline. #5 (cost of living), #6 (early-career), #7 (sector pace)
Regional transition fund Per role automated, allocate to local retraining and stipends — often pooled across employers in a region. #5, #10, plus local-area outcomes (above)
Reply with your 3–5 picks. Or fewer, or more, or a totally different set — whichever helps us land on the most useful framing for the panel. Suggestions for swaps welcome (the "Other candidates" box above lists a few I considered but didn't include). Thanks for the time.
